cards.q: What is LACP and what standard defines it?
cards.a: LACP (Link Aggregation Control Protocol) is the IEEE-standard EtherChannel negotiation protocol, originally IEEE 802.3ad and now IEEE 802.1AX. It dynamically negotiates multiple physical interfaces into one logical Port-Channel for increased bandwidth, redundancy, and a single logical Layer-2/Layer-3 interface.

cards.q: What are LACP's two negotiation modes and how does negotiation work?
cards.a: active: actively sends LACP PDUs and can form with active or passive. passive: waits for LACP PDUs and responds, forming with active only. At least one side must be active for a bundle to form.

cards.q: Which LACP mode combinations form a bundle?
cards.a: active + active = Yes; active + passive = Yes; passive + active = Yes; passive + passive = No. At least one side must be active.

cards.q: Why does passive + passive not form an LACP bundle?
cards.a: Because neither side initiates LACP negotiation (no side actively sends the LACP PDUs needed to start the bundle).

cards.q: Is Cisco `on` an LACP mode?
cards.a: No. `on` is not an LACP mode; it creates a static EtherChannel with no negotiation protocol.

cards.q: What EtherType carries LACP, and under what protocol class does it run?
cards.a: LACP is carried as an IEEE Slow Protocol using EtherType 0x8809.

cards.q: What are LACP's fast and slow PDU intervals?
cards.a: Fast LACP = 1 second; Slow LACP = 30 seconds. Do not memorize LACP as universally 1-second PDUs.

cards.q: What information is exchanged in LACP PDUs?
cards.a: Actor System ID, Partner System ID, Actor/Partner Key, Port Priority, Port Number, and LACP state information.

cards.q: What is the LACP System ID and how is it prioritized?
cards.a: It is System Priority + System MAC Address. Lower system priority is preferred when determining the LACP system relationship.

cards.q: What is the difference between LACP System Priority and Port Priority?
cards.a: System Priority helps determine LACP system selection. Port Priority helps select member ports when there are more eligible links than the active-member limit.

cards.q: Should you memorize a universal active-member limit for LACP?
cards.a: No. Exact active-member limits are platform-dependent; do not memorize a universal '8 active / 16 total' rule for all Cisco platforms.

cards.q: What command creates an LACP EtherChannel?
cards.a: channel-group 1 mode active on each physical interface, which associates the interface with EtherChannel 1, enables LACP active mode, and creates/binds the logical Port-channel1 interface.

cards.q: What is the recommended EtherChannel configuration model?
cards.a: Configure the logical Port-channel1 interface with the common bundle behavior (e.g., switchport mode trunk, allowed VLANs) and keep physical member interfaces compatible.

cards.q: Is `switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q` always required?
cards.a: No. It is platform-dependent; on platforms where 802.1Q is the only supported trunk encapsulation, the command may not exist.

cards.q: Does EtherChannel normally send every packet round-robin across all links?
cards.a: No. EtherChannel calculates a hash from selected packet fields and uses the result to choose a member link. A single flow normally remains on one physical member, preventing packet reordering.

cards.q: What fields can EtherChannel hash inputs include?
cards.a: Source MAC, Destination MAC, source+destination MAC, Source IP, Destination IP, source+destination IP, Layer-4 source/destination ports, and other platform-supported combinations.

cards.q: Does one TCP flow get the full aggregate of a 4-link EtherChannel?
cards.a: No. A 4 × 1-Gbps EtherChannel has about 4 Gbps aggregate capacity, but a single flow typically uses one 1-Gbps member; multiple flows are distributed across members.

cards.q: What parameter consistency is required among EtherChannel members?
cards.a: Speed, duplex, switchport mode, access VLAN (when used), native VLAN (for trunks), allowed VLANs, trunk configuration, Layer-3 configuration (for L3 EtherChannels), and compatible EtherChannel protocol/mode. Exact checks are platform and configuration dependent.

cards.q: How does STP view an EtherChannel?
cards.a: STP treats the EtherChannel as one logical link/port. It does not normally see the member interfaces as separate Layer-2 paths, preventing STP from blocking individual members of the same EtherChannel.

cards.q: In `show etherchannel summary`, what do SU and P mean?
cards.a: S = Layer-2 EtherChannel; U = in use. P means the port is bundled in the port-channel. P does not mean 'LACP negotiated'.

cards.q: What do the EtherChannel flags I, D, and s mean?
cards.a: I = Stand-alone; D = Down; s = Suspended. The exact flag set and interpretation should be read from the platform's command output.

cards.q: Which commands verify an LACP EtherChannel?
cards.a: show etherchannel summary; show etherchannel 1 port-channel; show lacp neighbor; show lacp counters; show lacp sys-id; show etherchannel load-balance.

cards.q: What is the troubleshooting order for an LACP EtherChannel that will not form?
cards.a: Physical layer → LACP mode → EtherChannel membership (show etherchannel summary) → member consistency (speed/duplex/VLAN/trunk) → Port-channel state → LACP neighbor → load balancing.

cards.q: When is `show lacp sys-id` useful?
cards.a: For viewing the local LACP system identifier on platforms that support the command.

cards.q: A member shows flag I — what does it indicate and what should you check?
cards.a: I = Stand-alone. Likely cause is LACP mode/compatibility; check LACP mode (e.g., ensure not passive + passive) and member compatibility.

cards.q: What is the most important CCNP LACP rule?
cards.a: ACTIVE + ACTIVE = BUNDLE; ACTIVE + PASSIVE = BUNDLE; PASSIVE + PASSIVE = NO BUNDLE; ON = STATIC / NO LACP.

cards.q: What are the key LACP quick-review facts?
cards.a: IEEE 802.3ad/802.1AX; modes active/passive; forms active↔active/passive, not passive↔passive; EtherType 0x8809; fast 1 s, slow 30 s; System ID = priority+MAC; hash-based per-flow load balancing; STP sees one logical port; on = static.

cards.q: Compare LACP, PAgP, and static `on`.
cards.a: LACP: IEEE standard, negotiates, active/passive, multi-vendor, modern choice. PAgP: Cisco proprietary, negotiates, desirable/auto, Cisco-only, legacy. on: no standard, no negotiation, static, must be manually consistent.
